new_statements.translation: 1123. From the point of view of word accent, Pomeranian divides into two parts, of course not very sharply separated from each other: in one area the accent is free and mobile, in the other it is bound to the first syllable of the word. [...] 1124. As dialects with free and partly also mobile accent one must count the North Pomeranian and South Kashubian dialects, except the Parchowo dialect and the South-West Kashubian dialects; as dialects with immobile initial accent, the Parchowo dialect, the South-West Kashubian dialects, the Kashubian-Zaborian transitional dialects and the Zaborian ones. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Slovincian has an empty rule; this work supplies it: free, mobile (lexical/morphological) accent for the Slovincian dialects, as part of the North Pomeranian free-accent zone, against fixed initial accent in the southern zone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Slovincian belongs to the North Pomeranian group, where word accent is free (not tied to any syllable) and mobile within paradigms; fixed initial accent holds only in the southern group (Parchowo, SW Kashubian, transitional and Zaborian dialects), and Polish penultimate accent is spreading into the Zaborian border dialects (§ 1126, p. 605). § 1128 (p. 606): the mobile type with accent on the final suffix syllable in certain cases 'w większym zakresie jest tylko w gwarach słowińskich, główczyckiej, cecenowskiej i charbrowsko-łebskiej, jak również w jastarnickiej oraz w Kuzwelcie' (to a larger extent only in the Slovincian, Główczyce, Cecenowo and Charbrowo-Łeba dialects, and in Jastarnia and Kuzfeld).
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 1186, p. 642: in runs of three or more unstressed syllables the penultimate is regularly the strongest ('regularnie zgłoska przedostatnia jest najsilniejsza.. Ten przycisk poboczny na zgłosce przedostatniej jest właściwy wszystkim pomorskim gwarom'); a second, much stronger secondary accent occurs in compounds of two polysyllabic words, each member keeping its accent, one main and one secondary (§§ 1186-1187, pp. 642-643); p. 646: in polysyllabic pronoun + noun groups the pronoun's accent is weaker, 'akcentem pobocznym, co jednak na pewno stwierdziłem tylko dla słowińszczyzny' (confirmed with certainty only for Slovincian).
new_statements.exceptions: Vocative names and animal calls with final accent in southern dialects (§ 1125); Polish penultimate accent in Zaborian border dialects (§ 1126); many class-specific accent alternations for Slovincian and its neighbours throughout §§ 1127-1185 (nouns, adjectives, numerals, pronouns, verbs), with cross-references to Slovinzische Grammatik pp. 172 ff., 178, 187, 190.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog item kash1274 is named Slovincian, but Glottolog kash1274 is Kashubian; Slovincian proper (Kluki/Smołdzino area, extinct) is slov1270. Lorentz 1927-37 treats the 'gwary słowińskie' as part of North Pomeranian and groups them with the Główczyce, Cecenowo and Charbrowo-Łeba dialects (the four dialects on German Pomerania) for the accent-quality and mobile-accent facts; Lorentz 1903 describes West and East Slovincian (Gardna and Smołdzino/Kluki). Hopkins 2001 lists Slovincian as dialect I of North Kashubian and gives no Slovincian-specific stress rule.

new_statements.quote: Most descriptions of Kashubian stress focus on the northern dialects and adopt a historical perspective, making determination of the default stress pattern difficult, but Kashubian can be characterized on the whole, as I have argued in Hopkins (1991, 1992), as having primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological or morphological word, with lexically stressed morphemes drawing stress away from this initial position. [...] There is little evidence for secondary stress: Lorentz (1925: 93) claims it falls on the initial syllable of compounds and the penultimate syllable of longer words with initial primary stress, but he does not mark it in his transcriptions of Kashubian speech

new_statements.relation_note: A whole-language generalization (default initial + lexical stress) that reframes Lorentz's northern 'free, mobile' accent as lexical stress overriding an initial default; it adds domain and secondary-stress detail but gives no Slovincian-specific placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Kashubian as a whole (Slovincian counted as dialect I of North Kashubian in his table, p. 26): default primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological/morphological word, overridden by lexically stressed morphemes; stress domain = clitic group in the south, prosodic word in the north; a trochaic foot is built over the lexically stressed syllable or else the first syllable; no rhythmic secondary stress, so no exhaustive footing. Slovincian itself is not described; Hopkins refers the compiler to Lorentz 1903 and Stokhof 1973 (Kluki dialect, p. 12).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'There is little evidence for secondary stress' (p. 31); cites Lorentz 1925: 93 for secondary stress on the initial syllable of compounds and the penult of longer initially-stressed words, unmarked in Lorentz's transcriptions and only sporadic in the AJK and Topolinska.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically stressed morphemes; prepositions often (esp. southern dialects) included in the stress domain of the following word.

new_statements.quote: Der Wortakzent des Slovinzischen ist frei, d. h. er ist nicht wie der des Polnischen und Čechischen an eine bestimmte Silbe gebunden. Auch darin ist er unbeschränkt, dass er auf jede beliebige Silbe des Worts fallen kann und nicht etwa wie der des Griechischen an eine bestimmte Silbenzahl gebunden ist. In den einzelnen Paradigmen ist ein reger Akzentwechsel vorhanden. Es ist jedoch eine Tendenz zu bemerken, bei mehrsilbigen Stämmen, besonders in der Substantiv-, seltener in der Verbalflexion, den Akzent auf der ersten Silbe festzulegen.
new_statements.translation: The word accent of Slovincian is free, i.e. it is not, like that of Polish and Czech, bound to a particular syllable. It is also unrestricted in that it can fall on any syllable of the word whatsoever and is not, like that of Greek, bound to a particular number of syllables. Within the individual paradigms there is lively accent alternation. A tendency can however be noted, in polysyllabic stems, especially in noun and more rarely in verb inflection, to fix the accent on the first syllable. (scanned normalized: 'ist ist' and 'festzniegcn' in the djvu text read 'ist' and 'festzulegen'.)

new_statements.relation_note: The primary description of Slovincian proper (slov1270), cited by both Lorentz 1927-37 and Hopkins 2001; agrees with index 0 that Slovincian accent is free and mobile.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Free, mobile word accent, any syllable possible, with paradigmatic alternation and a tendency toward stem-initial fixing in polysyllabic stems; § 99 p. 171: end-stressed forms occur only with monosyllabic stems, and in polysyllabic stems the accent may not move beyond the last stem syllable. Two accent qualities (scharfer Ton on long-grade vowels, dehnender Ton on short-grade vowels), §§ 95-97.
new_statements.secondary_stress: § 108 p. 219: 'In einstämmigen nichtzusammengesetzten Wörtern ist nur eine Silbe durch den Akzent ausgezeichnet'; secondary accents only in compounds of two polysyllabic words (each keeps its accent, one main, one secondary), in va- prefixed nouns, in adjective compounds, and on the penult of superlatives of more than three syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Sporadic initial-accent forms that sound like speech errors (§ 98); the § 108 compound patterns.

new_statements.quote: 2. Hinsichtlich des Wortakzents zerfällt das Pomor. in zwei, allerdings nicht scharf von einander geschiedene Teile: in dem einen ist der Akzent frei und beweglich, in dem andern ist er an die erste Silbe des Wortes gebunden. Im großen ganzen ist jenes der Fall im Npomor. und Skasch. mit Ausnahme des Parch. D. und Swk., dies im Par. D., Swk., Übg. und Sabor. Der Übergang erfolgt allmählich, zuerst schwindet die Endbetonung, und zwar bis auf einige wenige Fälle noch innerhalb des Npomor., dann folgt die Fixierung des Akzents auf der Anfangssilbe. [...] [p. 94:] Im Slz., Glow. und Zez. D. ist die Endbetonung in allen genannten Formen vorhanden, nur der Dat. Plur. zeigt öfters Schwanken.
new_statements.translation: 2. As regards word accent, Pomoranian falls into two parts, though not sharply separated from one another: in the one the accent is free and mobile, in the other it is bound to the first syllable of the word. By and large the former is the case in North Pomoranian [= Slovincian + North Kashubian] and South Kashubian except the Parchau dialect and Southwest Kashubian, the latter in the Parchau dialect, Southwest Kashubian, the transitional dialects and Saborian. The transition is gradual: first final stress disappears, apart from a few cases still within North Pomoranian, then follows the fixing of the accent on the initial syllable. [...] [p. 94:] In Slovincian and the Glowitz and Zezenow dialects final stress is present in all the forms named [the mobile-paradigm case forms]; only the dative plural often wavers.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Slovincian (Slz., Lorentz's division I.A of North Pomoranian) has a free and mobile word accent inherited from the Proto-Slavic free accent: stress may fall on any syllable, its position is a property of the word/stem class, and it shifts within paradigms by morphological category (par. 74-79 give the accent types for nouns, adjectives, numerals, pronouns, adverbs and verbs, e.g. type 1 fixed on the stem syllable vs. type 2 mobile with ending stress in Loc.sg -u, Instr.sg of a-/i-stems, Gen./Instr./Loc.pl etc.). Slovincian, with Glowitz, Zezenow and Charbrow-Leba, is the most conservative area, keeping ending stress in all the mobile forms. Southward through Kashubian ending stress is lost first and then the accent becomes fixed on the initial syllable (South Kashubian Parchau, SW Kashubian, transitional and Saborian dialects), with Polish-type stress intruding along the Pomoranian-Polish border (par. 80). Stress is predominantly expiratory; Slovincian additionally distinguishes two syllable-accent qualities tied to vowel length grade ('scharfer Ton' on long-grade, 'dehnender Ton' on short-grade vowels, par. 73.1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 93: 'Staerkere Nebenakzente haben im Allgemeinen die Komposita, deren Hauptakzent der urspruengliche des einen Gliedes ist.. und die Woerter, die den Akzent auf der ersten Silbe haben und mehr als drei Silben enthalten, also besonders die Superlative.. Meistens sind die Nebenakzente nur schwach. Ueber den slz. Nebenakzent s. Slz. Gram. 219 ff., die uebrigen Dialekte stimmen im ganzen damit ueberein.' Also p. 97: superlatives of more than three syllables mostly carry a secondary accent on the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Rufton (calling contour): a level drawn-out tone always on the LAST syllable with overlong vowel (Leosza-type vocatives), at least throughout South Pomoranian (p. 93); Slovincian tendency to eliminate ending stress in infinitives (only puoloc-type and -uc infinitives keep it, p. 101); perfective ve- compounds stress the prefix, preserved only in Slz., Glow., Zez., Ch.-L. (p. 99); in Slovincian the preposition takes the accent when the governed form has recessive accent, otherwise it is proclitic (par. 81, p. 104); accent shift onto the final syllable of 2sg imperatives before enclitics, very frequent in Slz. (p. 105); Lorentz 1903 already noted a sporadic tendency to fix the accent on the first syllable of polysyllabic stems, which the 1925 book frames as the southern development.
new_statements.identity_note: The work is a grammar of 'Pomoranian' = Slovincian + all Kashubian dialects; its statements are dialect-differentiated. Slovincian is Lorentz's 'Slz. = Slovinzisch (I. A)' (with Oslz./Weslz.), the westernmost division of Nordpomoranisch, grouped accentually with the Glowitz, Zezenow and Charbrow-Leba dialects as the most conservative free-accent area (material collected 1904-1913; the Vorwort notes some dialects had meanwhile disappeared). The catalog record is named Slovincian but keyed kash1274 (Glottolog Kashubian); the earlier reading's header notes Slovincian proper = slov1270. The reading 'lexical (unpredictable)' given here is for Slovincian (and North Kashubian); southern Kashubian dialects per the same work are fixed: initial syllable.

tone_statements.translation: Kashubian accent (GP 598-654, AJK X 1978 15-42) has the character of (dynamic) stress; in the north it is more dynamic and causes reductions of unstressed vowels, e.g. chałpa, glińca, Lëzno, nie chc (= nie chcã), rozmiôc, skorpa, srowi. Coastal Kashubian has kept the archaic free and partly mobile accent, e.g. czarownica, czarownic, czarownicama; here too the old accent on the final syllable (oxytonic) survives in disyllabic adjectives (e.g. miodny, mitczi) and adverbs (e.g. lepi, wczorô) ...

tone_statements.summary: Accent called dynamic stress ('przycisk'); nothing on pitch or tone, so the no-tone reading rests on that term. Stress marked by bold vowels in the HTML, lost in plain text; facts credited to GP, AJK.

readall_conflicts: No source places Slovincian stress on a fixed syllable. Lorentz 1903 (§ 98) and Lorentz 1927-37 (§§ 1123-1124, 1128) both describe the Slovincian dialects as having free, mobile accent with paradigmatic alternation, against fixed initial accent in the southern Kashubian/Zaborian group. Hopkins 2001 (pp. 30-31) reframes Kashubian as a whole as default initial stress overridden by lexically stressed morphemes, admits that the northern (free-accent) dialects make the default hard to determine, and defers Slovincian itself to Lorentz 1903 and Stokhof 1973; this is a difference of analysis (lexical stress over an initial default vs. free accent) rather than a contradiction about Slovincian placement. Lorentz 1925 could not be opened; Hopkins reports its p. 93 claim on secondary stress only. Lorentz 1927-37 (p. 642) and Lorentz 1903 (§ 108) agree that non-compound words carry one accent and that secondary accents arise in compounds; Lorentz 1927-37 adds a rhythmic penultimate secondary prominence in runs of three or more unstressed syllables in all Pomeranian dialects, which Hopkins calls 'little evidence for secondary stress'.

(2) Deciding source: a 392-page reference grammar with a full accent chapter, written by the fieldworker of a dialect that has since died out; WALS cites the same work; every later treatment I could see (Stokhof 1973 per Glottolog/Hopkins, Dogil per the StressTyp2 dump, Baerman 1999 and Hopkins 2001) reanalyses Lorentz rather than adding new first-hand data, so the best available description is held and quoted -> well-sourced.

sources.quote: § 98. Vorbemerkung. Der Wortakzent des Slovinzischen ist frei, d. b. er ist nicht wie der des Polnischen and Cechischen an eine bestimmte Silbe gebunden. Auch darin ist ist er unbeschrankt, dass er auf jede beliebige Silbe des Worts fallen kann und nicbt etwa wie der des Griechischen an eine bestimmte Silbenzahl gebunden ist. In den einzelnen Paradigmen ist ein reger Akzentwecbsel vorhanden. Es ist jedoch eine Tendenz zu bemerken, bei mehrsilbigen Stammen, besonders in der Substantiv-, seltener in der Verbalflexion, den Akzent auf der ersten Silbe festzulegen. Irgend etwas Bestimmtes hieriiber zu sagen, ist nicht moglich, da derartig betonte Formen nur sehr vereinzelt auftreten und meistens den Eindruck eines Sprechfehlers machen ... § 99. sources.quote: Most descriptions of Kashubian stress focus on the northern dialects and adopt a historical perspective, making determination of the default stress pattern difficult, but Kashubian can be characterized on the whole, as I have argued in Hopkins (1991, 1992), as having primary stress on the first syllable of the phonological or morphological word, with lexically stressed morphemes drawing stress away from this initial position. [...] There is little evidence for secondary stress: Lorentz (1925: 93) claims it falls on the initial syllable of compounds and the penultimate syllable of longer words with initial primary stress, but he does not mark it in his transcriptions of Kashubian speech

Hinsichtlich des Wortakzents zerfällt das Pomor. in zwei, allerdings nicht scharf von einander geschiedene Teile: in dem einen ist der Akzent frei und beweglich, in dem andern ist er an die erste Silbe des Wortes gebunden. sources.quote: Dialects of Central Kashubian fall into two groups regarding the stress pattern. In system I, stress is fixed on the same syllable in a paradigm, e.g. /tʃaˈrɔvɲits-a/ ‘witch’ n.sg., /tʃaˈrɔvɲits-ama/ instr.pl., /tʃaˈrɔvɲits/ g.pl. In system II, stress is word-initial, e.g. /ˈjaskuwk-a/ ‘swallow’ n.sg., /ˈjaskuwk-ama/ instr.pl. (Breza & Treder 1981: 20–21). [fn. 7, p. 301:] Second, modern Central Kashubian does not show a regular pattern of penultimate stress; see Section 2.

tone.translation: Kashubian accent (GP 598-654, AJK X 1978 15-42) has the character of (dynamic) stress; in the north it is more dynamic and causes reductions of unstressed vowels, e.g. chałpa, glińca, Lëzno, nie chc (= nie chcã), rozmiôc, skorpa, srowi. Coastal Kashubian has kept the archaic free and partly mobile accent, e.g. czarownica, czarownic, czarownicama; here too the old accent on the final syllable (oxytonic) survives in disyllabic adjectives (e.g. miodny, mitczi) and adverbs (e.g. lepi, wczorô) ...

tone.quote: Among word-individualizing factors the most important is stress. A word can be defined phonologically as a sequence of syllables one and only one of which bears the stress. In the system under discussion, in terms of syllabic word structure the stress is free. That is to say that any syllable in a word can bear the stress, the place of stress is morphologically defined and thus distinctive on the morphological level. ... As far as quantity is concerned, there are in general no limitations in the arrangement or the number of long syllables in the word. This is why quantity can be treated consistently as a segmental distinctive feature.

Obie nowsze intonacje są przy tym w pomorskim ściśle od siebie rozgraniczone iloczasem: przy intonacji nowoakutowej zgłoska akcentowana wykazuje samogłoskę na stopniu długim ..., przy nowocyrkumfleksowej na stopniu krótkim
tone.translation: For it turns out that the Pomeranian accent kept its old Proto-Slavic place only in metatonic positions, while in all others it retracted by one syllable towards the beginning of the word. ... The two newer intonations are moreover strictly distinguished from each other in Pomeranian by quantity: under neo-acute intonation the accented syllable shows the vowel in the long grade ..., under neo-circumflex in the short grade
